newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Germany to make EMU with bloated deficit - Ifo.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Germany to make EMU with bloated deficit - Ifo.

text.p: High unemployment and sluggish growth will push Bonn's budget deficit above the Maastricht target in 1997 but this will not stop Germany taking part in the planned euro single currency in 1999, the Ifo economic research institute said on Thursday.

Ifo said Germany's overall state budget deficit would be just under 120 billion marks ($69 billion), or 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, but said this did not take into account new savings measures being discussed.

"According to our forecast .... Germany will not meet the Maastricht reference target for the deficit ratio -- that is without the savings measures that are currently being planned in Bonn," Ifo President Karl-Heinrich Oppenlaender told the institute's annual meeting.
The Maastricht Treaty sets a ceiling of three percent for the deficit to GDP ratio of countries wishing to join the single currency, scheduled to start in January 1999.
With high unemployment levels draining funds from German government coffers, many independent analysts have said this target is very unlikely to be met.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel has insisted that the ceiling must be three percent and not above, arguing that allowing even a slight overshoot would pave the way for nations with much higher deficits to qualify, thereby weakening the euro.
But Oppenlaender said constant talk about figures behind the decimal point was misplaced.
"The public has the impression that even small decimal point divergences from the three percent level would endanger the stability of the future currency. This is wrong," he said.
"We should, therefore, end the decimal point discussion about this year's deficit as quickly as possible."
But the Ifo president warned Bonn against emergency or one-off measures, saying these were unnecessary and dangerous for credibility.

Commenting on a recent clash between Bonn and the Bundesbank over government plans to revalue and take a pay-out from central bank gold reserves, Oppenlaender said the battle had severely damaged the confidence of financial markets.
"Short-term measures to meet Maastricht Treaty reference targets at any price can destroy trust more than they can encourage it," he said.

The Ifo president said the stability of the euro currency was far more dependent on the monetary policy conducted by the European Central Bank (ECB) in 1999 and called for sustainable and solid fiscal policy to make that job easier.
"Politicians should concentrate first and foremost on achieving budgetary consolidation," Oppenlaender said.
In Germany, Ifo said that despite stubbornly high unemployment, healthy exports would help the overall economy to grow by between 2.0 and 2.5 percent in 1997.
Aided by the relatively soft level of the mark, exports are seeing good foreign demand, which should filter through to domestic demand over the year.
Ifo's business climate index for May, also released on Thursday, showed a slight pickup in confidence, driven mainly by improvements in the export sector.
The index rose to 95.3 in May from 94.7 in April, reaching the upper end of economists' forecasts.
"It's a good number. We are seeing an export-led recovery gaining strength," said Hans-Guenther Redeker, an economist at Chase Investment Bank in London.
Oppenlaender said this scenario was likely to remain in place for the time being, commenting: "As foreign orders figures show, exports will remain the driving force behind the German economy in 1997.
"The conditions for continued economic recovery are favourable. All in all we expect a rise in real GDP of between two to two and a half percent (in 1997)," he told the meeting.

But unemployment, currently running at 11.1 percent of the workforce or 4.26 million people, will not see any benefit from that growth this year, Oppenlaender said, with the average number out of work likely to rise by more than 300,000 to 4.3 million this year.
While this upward trend is forecast to turn tail next year, Oppenlaender said that average unemployment would still total 4.2 million in 1998.
